title: EU AI Act Article 26: What Deployers Must Do
context: 2026-08-28 engine cycle -- answer-first seed for deployer obligations under the EU AI Act; the Article 26 deployer duties became fully applicable on 2 August 2026 alongside the high-risk requirements they operationalise
body: Article 26 of the EU AI Act defines what a deployer -- the organisation using an AI system under its own authority, rather than the provider that built it -- must do. It became fully applicable on 2 August 2026, and it is the clause that turns high-risk obligations from a vendor promise into an operating duty. A deployer must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions of use; assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training, and authority; and, where the deployer exercises control over the input data, ensure that input data is relevant and sufficiently representative for the intended purpose. Deployers must monitor the operation of the system on the basis of the instructions of use and keep the automatically generated logs for the prescribed retention period, and they must inform workers and their representatives before putting a high-risk system into service in the workplace. Public bodies and certain private operators must also carry out a fundamental-rights impact assessment before deployment. The unifying idea is continuous, evidence-based supervision: a deployer is not asked to prove the system can never fail, but to show it is being watched. That is precisely the posture the Council of AI codifies as monitored containment, not provable isolation -- a signed, running record of measurement, monitoring, and containment events that demonstrates oversight rather than claiming an impossible guarantee. A verified measurement credential over those records gives a deployer the objective, attributable evidence to show Article 26 duties are discharged in fact, not just asserted.
